summary: This paper presents a computationally efficient method for constructing detector error models (DEMs) that accurately capture the effects of general Markovian circuit-level errors—including coherent and non-Pauli errors—on fault-tolerant quantum error correction, enabled by propagating errors through Clifford circuits using the elementary error generator (EEG) basis. The analysis shows that coherent errors can shift code thresholds, increase space-time costs for magic state cultivation, and boost logical error rates by up to an order of magnitude compared to equivalent stochastic Pauli errors, with validation on surface codes, bivariate bicycle codes, and $S$-state cultivation.
motivation: Quantum error correction protocols are traditionally designed and validated against Pauli stochastic error models, but real hardware exhibits coherent and non-Pauli errors from miscalibrated gates whose impacts on fault-tolerant quantum computing have been largely unpredictable due to exponential classical simulation cost.
method: The authors map arbitrary small Markovian circuit-level error models to DEMs by (1) representing errors as $\mathcal{E} = \exp(G)$ in the sparse EEG basis, (2) efficiently propagating EEGs through Clifford circuits, (3) combining errors using the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula, and (4) decomposing the circuit error generator by DEM event class using the Zassenhaus expansion, enabling accurate DEM construction with Monte Carlo estimation of logical error rates.
result: DEMs generated by this method predict syndrome and logical observable distributions with total variation distance $\sim 100\times$ smaller than Pauli-twirled models; surface code thresholds shift by $\sim 0.006$ CNOT infidelity depending on coherent error fraction; magic state cultivation logical error rates increase by $\approx 10\times$ for $35\%$ coherent $Z$-type error contributions, and certain coherent two-qubit errors are $15$–$28\%$ more damaging than stochastic equivalents.
